entries.lesson_core_move: Map each time feature in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) for a>1 and identify the resulting waveform as compressed toward t=0 with unchanged amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Recognizing x(at) as Time Compression for a>1

prompt_blocks.text: For $y(t)=x(5t)$, which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: It is compressed toward $t=0$, and each time feature moves to one-fifth of its original time with unchanged amplitude.
It is expanded away from $t=0$, and each time feature moves to five times its original time.
It is shifted right by $5$, and each time feature moves $5$ units later.
It is scaled vertically by $5$, and each amplitude becomes $5$ times larger.
It is time-reversed, and each feature time changes sign.

questions.correct_answer: It is compressed toward $t=0$, and each time feature moves to one-fifth of its original time with unchanged amplitude.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $5>1$, the factor inside $x(5t)$ makes time run faster. The signal is compressed toward $t=0$.
So every feature moves to one-fifth of its original time, and the amplitude stays the same.

prompt_blocks.text: If $y(t)=x(3t)$ and $x(t)$ has a peak at $t_0=9$, where does the peak appear in $y(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: At $t=3$, with the same amplitude.
At $t=27$, with the same amplitude.
At $t=6$, because the signal is shifted right by $3$.
At $t=-3$, because the signal is time-reversed.
At $t=9$, but its amplitude becomes $3$ times larger.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the original peak time by setting the inside argument equal to $9$.
That gives $t=3$. Since $3>1$, the peak is compressed toward $t=0$, not shifted, reversed, or rescaled in amplitude.

sections.section_title: Mapping a Single Time Feature Under Compression

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=8$, where does that peak appear in $y(t)=x(4t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the input is $x(4t)$, match the same feature by solving $4t=8$. That gives $t=2$, so the peak moves to $t=2$ while its height stays the same.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ has a valley at $t=9$, where does that valley appear in $y(t)=x(3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the input is $x(3t)$, match the same feature by solving $3t=9$. That gives $t=3$, so the valley moves toward $t=0$ and only its time location changes.

sections.section_title: Compressing Support Intervals and Durations

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[3,9]$, what is the support of $y(t)=x(3t)$, and how does its duration change?

choice_blocks.text: The support is $[1,3]$, and the duration changes from $6$ to $2$, so it is one-third as long.
The support is $[9,27]$, and the duration changes from $6$ to $18$.
The support is $[3,9]$, and the duration stays $6$.
The support is $[3,1]$, and the interval order is reversed.
The support is $[6,12]$, as if the signal were shifted right instead of scaled.

questions.correct_answer: The support is $[1,3]$, and the duration changes from $6$ to $2$, so it is one-third as long.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the argument is $x(3t)$, divide each support endpoint by $3$. So $3$ maps to $1$ and $9$ maps to $3$.
That gives support $[1,3]$. The duration drops from $9-3=6$ to $3-1=2$, while the amplitudes stay the same.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $(-4,8]$, what is the support of $y(t)=x(4t)$, and how does its duration change?

choice_blocks.text: The support is $(-1,2]$, and the duration changes from $12$ to $3$, so it is one-quarter as long.
The support is $(-16,32]$, and the duration changes from $12$ to $48$.
The support is $(-4,8]$, and the duration stays $12$.
The support is $(2,-1]$, and the interval order is reversed.
The support is $[0,12]$, as if the signal were shifted instead of scaled.

questions.correct_answer: The support is $(-1,2]$, and the duration changes from $12$ to $3$, so it is one-quarter as long.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the argument is $x(4t)$, divide each endpoint by $4$ and keep the open or closed endpoint type the same. So $-4$ maps to $-1$ and $8$ maps to $2$.
That gives support $(-1,2]$. The duration drops from $8-(-4)=12$ to $2-(-1)=3$, while the amplitudes stay the same.

sections.section_title: Reading a Compressed Waveform with Unchanged Amplitudes

prompt_blocks.text: A waveform $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=6$ and is nonzero on $[2,14]$. What best describes $y(t)=x(2t)$?

choice_blocks.text: The peak moves to $t=3$, the support becomes $[1,7]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
The peak moves to $t=12$, the support becomes $[4,28]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
The peak moves to $t=3$, the support becomes $[1,7]$, and the amplitudes are doubled.
The peak stays at $t=6$, the support stays $[2,14]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
The peak moves to $t=-3$, the support becomes $[-7,-1]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.

questions.correct_answer: The peak moves to $t=3$, the support becomes $[1,7]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $y(t)=x(2t)$ has factor $2>1$, it is compressed toward $t=0$. So every time coordinate is halved: the peak at $6$ moves to $3$, and the support $[2,14]$ moves to $[1,7]$. The amplitudes do not change.

prompt_blocks.text: A waveform $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=9$ and is nonzero on $[3,15]$. What best describes $y(t)=x(3t)$?

choice_blocks.text: The peak moves to $t=3$, the support becomes $[1,5]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
The peak moves to $t=27$, the support becomes $[9,45]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
The peak moves to $t=3$, the support becomes $[1,5]$, and the amplitudes are tripled.
The peak stays at $t=9$, the support stays $[3,15]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.
The peak moves to $t=-3$, the support becomes $[-5,-1]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.

questions.correct_answer: The peak moves to $t=3$, the support becomes $[1,5]$, and the amplitudes stay the same.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $y(t)=x(3t)$ has factor $3>1$, it is compressed toward $t=0$. So every time coordinate is divided by $3$: the peak at $9$ moves to $3$, and the support $[3,15]$ moves to $[1,5]$. The amplitudes remain unchanged.

entries.lesson_core_move: Map each time feature in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) for 0<a<1 and identify the resulting waveform as expanded away from t=0 with unchanged amplitudes.

sections.section_title: Recognizing x(t/2) as a Time Expansion

prompt_blocks.text: Which transformed signal is a time expansion of $x(t)$ by factor $3$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time expansion by factor $3$ uses $x(t/3)$, because $x(at)$ with $a=1/3$ has $0<a<1$. Every time feature moves to $t_0/a=3t_0$, and the amplitudes stay the same.

prompt_blocks.text: Which transformed signal is a time expansion of $x(t)$ by factor $4$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time expansion by factor $4$ uses $x(t/4)$, because $x(at)$ with $a=1/4$ is still in the case $0<a<1$. That means every time feature moves to $t_0/a=4t_0$ while its amplitude stays unchanged.

sections.section_title: Mapping Original Time Points to t0/a

prompt_blocks.text: A feature is located at $t_0=7$ in $x(t)$. If the signal becomes $x(t/4)$, where does that feature move?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $x(t/4)$ is $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{4}$. The rule is $t_0 \mapsto t_0/a$, so $7/(1/4)=28$.

prompt_blocks.text: A feature is located at $t_0=-9$ in $x(t)$. If the signal becomes $x(t/3)$, where does that feature move?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $x(t/3)$ is $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{3}$. Apply $t_0 \mapsto t_0/a$: $-9/(1/3)=-27$, so the sign stays negative and the point moves farther from $t=0$.

sections.section_title: Finding Expanded Support with Unchanged Amplitude

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[2,10]$ and has peak amplitude $7$, what support interval and amplitude statement are correct for $x(t/2)$?

choice_blocks.text: The support is $[4,20]$ and the peak amplitude stays $7$.
The support is $[1,5]$ and the peak amplitude stays $7$.
The support is $[2,10]$ and the peak amplitude stays $7$.
The support is $[4,12]$ and the peak amplitude stays $7$.
The support is $[4,20]$ and the peak amplitude doubles to $14$.

questions.correct_answer: The support is $[4,20]$ and the peak amplitude stays $7$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor inside the argument is $\tfrac{1}{2}$, so write the signal as $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{2}$. For time expansion, each original time point moves to $t_{new}=t_0/a$.
So the endpoints $2$ and $10$ move to $4$ and $20$. The support expands away from $t=0$, and the amplitudes do not change.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero on $[-3,1]$ and has peak amplitude $4$, what support interval and amplitude statement are correct for $x(t/3)$?

choice_blocks.text: The support is $[-9,3]$ and the peak amplitude stays $4$.
The support is $[-1,\tfrac{1}{3}]$ and the peak amplitude stays $4$.
The support is $[-3,1]$ and the peak amplitude stays $4$.
The support is $[0,4]$ and the peak amplitude stays $4$.
The support is $[-9,3]$ and the peak amplitude doubles to $8$.

questions.correct_answer: The support is $[-9,3]$ and the peak amplitude stays $4$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor inside the argument is $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so write the signal as $x(at)$ with $a=\tfrac{1}{3}$. The mapping rule is still $t_{new}=t_0/a$.
So the endpoints $-3$ and $1$ move to $-9$ and $3$. The support expands away from $t=0$, and the amplitudes stay the same.

entries.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
entries.lesson_core_move: Map each key time point t0 in x(t) to t0/a in x(at) by solving at=t0, then use that mapping to relocate starts, stops, corners, peaks, and zero crossings.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping One Key Time Point in x(at)

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, a peak occurs at $t_0=10$. Where does that peak appear in $x(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue $2t$ and keep the same peak. Solve $2t=10$ for $t$.
So the peak appears at $t=5$ in $x(2t)$. The peak stays a peak; only its horizontal position changes.

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, a zero crossing occurs at $t_0=7$. Where does that zero crossing appear in $x(3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the cue $3t$ and keep the same zero crossing. Solve $3t=7$ for $t$.
So the zero crossing appears at $t=7/3$ in $x(3t)$. The crossing type stays the same; only the time coordinate is divided by the scale factor.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping Start and Stop Times

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, the signal is nonzero from $4$ to $12$. Where is it nonzero in $x(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve $2t=4$ to get $t=2$ and $2t=12$ to get $t=6$. So the nonzero interval in $x(2t)$ is $(2, 6)$.

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, the signal is nonzero from $1/2$ to $5/2$. Where is it nonzero in $x(4t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve $4t=1/2$ to get $t=1/8$ and $4t=5/2$ to get $t=5/8$. So the nonzero interval in $x(4t)$ is $(1/8, 5/8)$.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping Corners and Peaks

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, a piecewise waveform has a corner at $t=2$, a peak at $t=5$, and another corner at $t=8$. Where do these three features appear in $x(4t)$?

choice_blocks.text: corner at $t=8$, peak at $t=20$, corner at $t=32$
corner at $t=\frac{1}{2}$, peak at $t=\frac{5}{4}$, corner at $t=2$
corner at $t=2$, peak at $t=5$, corner at $t=8$
corner at $t=\frac{1}{2}$, corner at $t=2$, peak at $t=\frac{5}{4}$
corner at $t=\frac{1}{2}$, peak at $t=2$, corner at $t=\frac{5}{4}$

questions.correct_answer: corner at $t=\frac{1}{2}$, peak at $t=\frac{5}{4}$, corner at $t=2$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(4t)$, solve $4t=t_0$ for each labeled feature, so each original time is divided by $4$. That gives the corner at $t=\frac{1}{2}$, the peak at $t=\frac{5}{4}$, and the corner at $t=2$ in the same left-to-right order.

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, a piecewise waveform has a corner at $t=-6$, a peak at $t=-1$, and another corner at $t=9$. Where do these three features appear in $x(2t)$?

choice_blocks.text: corner at $t=-12$, peak at $t=-2$, corner at $t=18$
corner at $t=-\frac{1}{2}$, peak at $t=-3$, corner at $t=\frac{9}{2}$
corner at $t=-3$, corner at $t=-\frac{1}{2}$, peak at $t=\frac{9}{2}$
corner at $t=-3$, peak at $t=-\frac{1}{2}$, corner at $t=\frac{9}{2}$
corner at $t=-3$, peak at $t=-1$, corner at $t=\frac{9}{2}$

questions.correct_answer: corner at $t=-3$, peak at $t=-\frac{1}{2}$, corner at $t=\frac{9}{2}$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(2t)$, divide each original time by $2$. The corner at $t=-6$ moves to $t=-3$, the peak at $t=-1$ moves to $t=-\frac{1}{2}$, and the corner at $t=9$ moves to $t=\frac{9}{2}$, so the left-to-right order stays the same.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Mapping Zero Crossings

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, the signal crosses zero at $t=-8$, $t=0$, and $t=12$. Where are the zero crossings in $x(4t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(4t)$, solve $4t=t_0$ for each zero crossing, so each original time is divided by $4$. That gives $t=-2$, $t=0$, and $t=3$. The origin stays fixed.

prompt_blocks.text: In $x(t)$, the signal crosses zero at $t=-8$, $t=-2$, $t=0$, and $t=6$. Where are the zero crossings in $x(\frac{1}{2}t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(\frac{1}{2}t)$, solve $\frac{1}{2}t=t_0$ for each zero crossing. That doubles every original time, so the crossings move to $t=-16$, $t=-4$, $t=0$, and $t=12$. The origin still stays fixed.

sections.lesson_title: How Time Scaling Moves Key Time Points
sections.section_title: Rebuilding a Scaled Time Axis from Key Points

prompt_blocks.text: A signal in $x(t)$ has key points at $t=6$ (stop time), $t=-9$ (zero crossing), $t=3$ (peak), and $t=-3$ (corner). Rebuild the key-point axis for $x(3t)$.

choice_blocks.text: $-3$ (zero crossing) < $-1$ (corner) < $1$ (peak) < $2$ (stop time)
$2$ (stop time) < $-3$ (zero crossing) < $1$ (peak) < $-1$ (corner)
$18$ (stop time) < $-27$ (zero crossing) < $9$ (peak) < $-9$ (corner)
$-3$ (zero crossing) < $-1$ (corner) < $1$ (peak)
$-3$ (zero crossing) < $-1$ (peak) < $1$ (corner) < $2$ (stop time)

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(3t)$, divide each original time by $3$: $6\mapsto 2$, $-9\mapsto -3$, $3\mapsto 1$, and $-3\mapsto -1$. Reordering left to right gives $-3$ (zero crossing) < $-1$ (corner) < $1$ (peak) < $2$ (stop time).

prompt_blocks.text: A signal in $x(t)$ has key points at $t=10$ (stop time), $t=-8$ (zero crossing), $t=-2$ (corner), and $t=6$ (peak). Rebuild the key-point axis for $x(4t)$.

choice_blocks.text: $5/2$ (stop time) < $-2$ (zero crossing) < $-1/2$ (corner) < $3/2$ (peak)
$-2$ (zero crossing) < $-1/2$ (corner) < $3/2$ (peak) < $5/2$ (stop time)
$40$ (stop time) < $-32$ (zero crossing) < $-8$ (corner) < $24$ (peak)
$-2$ (zero crossing) < $-1/2$ (corner) < $3/2$ (peak)
$-2$ (zero crossing) < $-1/2$ (peak) < $3/2$ (corner) < $5/2$ (stop time)

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(4t)$, divide each original time by $4$: $10\mapsto 5/2$, $-8\mapsto -2$, $-2\mapsto -1/2$, and $6\mapsto 3/2$. Reordering left to right gives $-2$ (zero crossing) < $-1/2$ (corner) < $3/2$ (peak) < $5/2$ (stop time).

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a piecewise signal x(t) into x(at) for a>0 by mapping each breakpoint t0 to t0/a and replacing t with at in the formula assigned to each scaled interval.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Breakpoints of a Simple Piecewise Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise definition is $x(4t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve $4t=8$ to get the new breakpoint $t=2$. Time scaling moves the breakpoint, but it does not change the piece values.
So the left piece stays $7$ and the right piece stays $-2$, with the breakpoint shifted from $8$ to $2$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise definition is $x(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve $2t=5$ to get the new breakpoint $t=\frac{5}{2}$. The only change is the breakpoint location; the piece values stay $1$ and $-5$.
So the transformed signal keeps the same values on each side, with the breakpoint divided by the scale factor.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Piecewise Formulas After Replacing t with at

prompt_blocks.text: What is $x(3t)$ for the signal below?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Divide each breakpoint by $3$, so $3$ becomes $1$ and $6$ becomes $2$. Then replace $t$ with $3t$ inside each formula: $t-2 \mapsto 3t-2$ and $8-t \mapsto 8-3t$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is $x(2t)$ for the signal below?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Divide each breakpoint by $2$, so $2$ becomes $1$ and $5$ becomes $5/2$. Then replace $t$ with $2t$ inside each formula: $2t+1 \mapsto 4t+1$ and $7-3t \mapsto 7-6t$.

sections.section_title: Time Compression of a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise definition is $x(3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve $3t=2$ and $3t=5$ to get the new breakpoints $t=\frac{2}{3}$ and $t=\frac{5}{3}$. Then replace $t$ with $3t$ in the nonconstant piece.
The constant pieces stay $0$ and $7$, so the only formula that changes is the middle one: $t+1 \mapsto 3t+1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Which piecewise definition is $x(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve $2t=-2$, $2t=1$, and $2t=3$ to get the new breakpoints $t=-1$, $t=\frac{1}{2}$, and $t=\frac{3}{2}$. Then replace $t$ with $2t$ in the middle formula.
The constant pieces stay $1$, $4$, and $-1$, while $t+2$ becomes $2t+2$ after substitution.

sections.section_title: Time Expansion of a Multi-Interval Piecewise Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the correct piecewise definition of $x(t/3)$ for the signal below.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor inside the argument is $1/3$, so this is an expansion by $3$. Move the breakpoints from $-2$ and $4$ to $-6$ and $12$, then replace $t$ by $t/3$ in the middle formula.

prompt_blocks.text: Choose the correct piecewise definition of $x(t/5)$ for the signal below.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor inside the argument is $1/5$, so the signal expands by $5$. Move the breakpoints from $1$ and $4$ to $5$ and $20$, then evaluate the middle interval at $t/5$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert time-scaled exponentials by rewriting e^{s(at)} as e^{(as)t} and interpreting a as changing the growth, decay, or oscillation rate in continuous time.

sections.section_title: Rewriting a Time-Scaled Real Exponential

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{-4(3t)}$ in standard form and state how its decay compares with $e^{-4t}$.

choice_blocks.text: $e^{-4(3t)}$; the decay is three times as fast.
$e^{-12t}$; the decay is three times as fast.
$e^{-4t}$; the decay is three times as fast.
$e^{-(4/3)t}$; the decay is three times as fast.
$e^{-12t}$; the decay is three times as slow.

questions.correct_answer: $e^{-12t}$; the decay is three times as fast.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the exponent coefficient by the time-scale factor inside the parentheses.
This becomes $x(t)=e^{-12t}$. Compared with $e^{-4t}$, the coefficient magnitude triples, so the decay is three times as fast.

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{-6(0.5t)}$ in standard form and state how its decay compares with $e^{-6t}$.

choice_blocks.text: $e^{-6t}$; the decay is slower.
$e^{-12t}$; the decay is slower.
$e^{-6(0.5t)}$; the decay is slower.
$e^{-3t}$; the decay is slower.
$e^{-3t}$; the decay is faster.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A factor of $0.5$ inside the exponent halves the exponent coefficient.
This becomes $x(t)=e^{-3t}$. Compared with $e^{-6t}$, the coefficient magnitude is smaller, so the decay is slower.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Faster and Slower Exponential Decay

prompt_blocks.text: For $x_1(t)=e^{-4(2t)}$, $x_2(t)=e^{-4t}$, and $x_3(t)=e^{-4(0.25t)}$, which signal decays fastest?

choice_blocks.text: $x_2(t)$ and $x_3(t)$ tie for fastest
All three decay at the same rate

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the base decay coefficient by the scale factor: $x_1(t)=e^{-8t}$, $x_2(t)=e^{-4t}$, and $x_3(t)=e^{-t}$. The most negative exponent coefficient decays fastest, so $x_1(t)$ is fastest.

prompt_blocks.text: Order these from fastest decay to slowest decay: $y_1(t)=e^{-2(1.5t)}$, $y_2(t)=e^{-2(0.5t)}$, $y_3(t)=e^{-2t}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite each signal by multiplying the base coefficient by the scale factor: $y_1(t)=e^{-3t}$, $y_2(t)=e^{-t}$, and $y_3(t)=e^{-2t}$. More negative means faster decay, so the order is $y_1(t)$, then $y_3(t)$, then $y_2(t)$.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Oscillation Rate of a Complex Exponential

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{j3(4t)}$ in standard form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the frequency coefficient $3$ by the time-scaling factor $4$. Since $3\cdot 4=12$, the rewritten signal is $e^{j12t}$, so the oscillation is faster.

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{j8(0.5t)}$ in standard form.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply the frequency coefficient $8$ by the scale factor $0.5$. Since $8\cdot 0.5=4$, the rewritten signal is $e^{j4t}$, so the oscillation is slower than $e^{j8t}$.

sections.section_title: Scaling Both the Envelope and Oscillation of a Damped Sinusoid

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite the damped sinusoid $x(t)=e^{(-2+j5)(3t)}$ in standard form and identify how both the envelope and oscillation compare with $e^{(-2+j5)t}$.

choice_blocks.text: $e^{(-6+j15)t}$; the envelope and oscillation are both 3 times faster.
$e^{(-6+j5)t}$; the envelope is 3 times faster, but the oscillation is unchanged.
$e^{(-2+j15)t}$; the envelope is unchanged, but the oscillation is 3 times faster.
$e^{(-\frac{2}{3}+j\frac{5}{3})t}$; the envelope and oscillation are both 3 times slower.
$e^{(-15+j6)t}$; the real and imaginary parts were swapped.

questions.correct_answer: $e^{(-6+j15)t}$; the envelope and oscillation are both 3 times faster.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply both parts of the exponent by $3$: $(-2+j5)(3t)=(-6+j15)t$. That makes the envelope decay 3 times faster and the oscillation rate 3 times faster.

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite the damped sinusoid $x(t)=e^{(-6+j8)(0.5t)}$ in standard form and identify how both the envelope and oscillation compare with $e^{(-6+j8)t}$.

choice_blocks.text: $e^{(-12+j16)t}$; the envelope and oscillation are both 2 times faster.
$e^{(-3+j8)t}$; the envelope is half as fast, but the oscillation is unchanged.
$e^{(-3+j4)t}$; the envelope and oscillation are both half as fast.
$e^{(-6+j4)t}$; the envelope is unchanged, but the oscillation is half as fast.
$e^{(-6+j16)t}$; only the oscillation changes.

questions.correct_answer: $e^{(-3+j4)t}$; the envelope and oscillation are both half as fast.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply both parts of the exponent by $0.5$: $(-6+j8)(0.5t)=(-3+j4)t$. So both the envelope and the oscillation slow down by a factor of $2$.

entries.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish time shifts from time scaling by mapping transformed arguments to key-time locations and deciding whether features translate by a constant offset or compress/expand relative to t=0.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Time Shifts and Time Scaling
sections.section_title: Comparing One Key Time Under a Shift and a Scale

prompt_blocks.text: A signal $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=5$. Compare the peak location in $y_1(t)=x(t-1)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(2t)$.

choice_blocks.text: The peaks are at $t=6$ and $t=5/2$.
The peaks are at $t=4$ and $t=5/2$.
The peaks are at $t=6$ and $t=10$.
The peaks are at $t=4$ and $t=10$.
The peaks are at $t=5$ and $t=2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the inside argument to the original peak time $t=5$. For $y_1(t)=x(t-1)$, solve $t-1=5$ to get $t=6$. For $y_2(t)=x(2t)$, solve $2t=5$ to get $t=5/2$. The shift adds $1$; the scale divides the landmark time by $2$.

prompt_blocks.text: A signal $x(t)$ has a peak at $t=4$. Compare the peak location in $y_1(t)=x(t+3)$ and in $y_2(t)=x(3t)$.

choice_blocks.text: The peaks are at $t=1$ and $t=4/3$.
The peaks are at $t=7$ and $t=4/3$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Multiple Key Times Under a Shift and a Scale

prompt_blocks.text: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=1$, $t=3$, and $t=5$. Which answer choice correctly lists the corresponding key times in $x(t-3)$ and $x(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add $3$ to each key time for $x(t-3)$, so $1,3,5$ becomes $4,6,8$. Divide each key time by $2$ for $x(2t)$, so $1,3,5$ becomes $0.5,1.5,2.5$. The shift keeps the gaps the same, while the scale halves them.

prompt_blocks.text: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=0$, $t=4$, and $t=10$. Which answer choice correctly lists the corresponding key times in $x(t-3)$ and $x(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add $3$ to each key time for $x(t-3)$, so $0,4,10$ becomes $3,7,13$. Divide each key time by $2$ for $x(2t)$, so $0,4,10$ becomes $0,2,5$. The shift preserves the gaps, while the scale compresses them toward $t=0$.

prompt_blocks.text: The signal $x(t)$ has key times at $t=2$ and $t=6$. One candidate transformed signal has them at $t=5$ and $t=9$; another has them at $t=1$ and $t=3$. Which choice correctly identifies the translation and the compression, and gives the matching offset or factor?

choice_blocks.text: Candidate 1 is a translation by $3$ and candidate 2 is a compression by factor $2$.
Candidate 1 is a compression by factor $2$ and candidate 2 is a translation by $3$.
Candidate 1 is a translation by $2$ and candidate 2 is a compression by factor $3$.
Candidate 1 is a translation by $-3$ and candidate 2 is an expansion by factor $2$.
Candidate 1 is an expansion by factor $2$ and candidate 2 is a compression by factor $3$.

questions.correct_answer: Candidate 1 is a translation by $3$ and candidate 2 is a compression by factor $2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The original spacing is $6-2=4$. Candidate 1 keeps the spacing at $9-5=4$, so it is a translation by $3$. Candidate 2 changes the spacing to $3-1=2$, which is half of the original gap, so it is a compression by factor $2$.

questions.correct_answer: $y_1(t)$ has breakpoints at $t=1$ and $t=5$, and $y_2(t)$ has breakpoints at $t=-1/3$ and $t=1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A shift by $2$ adds $2$ to both breakpoints, so $x(t-2)$ turns on from $t=1$ to $t=5$. For $x(3t)$, solve $3t=-1$ and $3t=3$, giving $t=-1/3$ and $t=1$. The shift translates both endpoints; the scale divides the breakpoint locations by $3$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-t}$, the value $e^{-3}$ occurs at $t=3$. Which answer choice gives the correct times at which that same level appears in $x(t-2)$ and in $x(3t)$, respectively?

choice_blocks.text: $x(t-2)$ reaches the level at $t=5$ and $x(3t)$ reaches it at $t=1$.
$x(t-2)$ reaches the level at $t=1$ and $x(3t)$ reaches it at $t=1$.
$x(t-2)$ reaches the level at $t=5$ and $x(3t)$ reaches it at $t=3/2$.
$x(t-2)$ reaches the level at $t=3$ and $x(3t)$ reaches it at $t=1$.
$x(t-2)$ reaches the level at $t=5$ and $x(3t)$ reaches it at $t=3/5$.

questions.correct_answer: $x(t-2)$ reaches the level at $t=5$ and $x(3t)$ reaches it at $t=1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The reference level $e^{-3}$ occurs at $t=3$ in $x(t)=e^{-t}$. A shift by $2$ moves that time to $3+2=5$, and a scale by $3$ moves it to $3/3=1$. A shift translates by a constant offset, while a scale compresses by the reciprocal factor.
